newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singaporean denies U.S. insider trading - papers.
newsitem.headline: Singaporean denies U.S. insider trading - papers.

text.p: Singapore businessman Raymond Lum Kwan Sung has denied allegations of insider trading made by the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Singapore newspapers said on Monday.
The daily Straits Times and Business Times both said they had received a fax from Lum denying the allegations and saying he "will strenuously resist the spurious allegations".
Lum, who is chairman of Lum Chang Holdings Ltd, could not be reached immediately for comment on the reports, which also said that he would be consulting with his lawyers.
The insider trading charges relate to the proposed takeover by Singapore-based Neptune Orient Lines of U.S.-based APL Ltd.
Over the weekend, NOL said in a statement that its senior executives had not spoken in months to Lum, and never talked to him about the takeover.

It said that in the course of their cooperation with the SEC investigation of alleged insider trading, "NOL senior executives have voluntarily responded to SEC inquiries about the acquisition, including informing the SEC that they have not spoken to Mr. Lum in several months and that they have never
spoken to Mr. Lum about the acquisition."
It said any implication to the contrary would be unfounded.
The SEC said on Friday it had added Lum as a defendant in the insider trading case involving APL Ltd securities.
In its civil case filed in U.S. District Court in Manhattan, the agency charged Lum with insider trading in APL, a provider of ocean-going cargo transportation services.
The SEC alleged that on February 25, Lum opened a trading account and between February 25 and March 18 purchased 190,100 APL shares representing a $4.4 million investment.
The SEC alleged Lum made an illegal profit after shares in APL rose on April 14 by $8.25 one day after APL announced it would be acquired by NOL for $825 million.

"After the transaction was announced, the value of Lum's investment increased by over $1.2 million, a 27 percent return in just under seven weeks. The Commission alleges that Lum Kwan Sung made his purchases of APL stock while in possession of material, nonpublic information about the transaction," the SEC said in its complaint.

The SEC said Lum "knows 'quite a few people' at the Singapore-based Neptune Orient, including two senior members of Neptune Orient's management who were intimately involved in the company's decision making and negotiations with respect to the acquisition."

In addition, the agency said Lum is executive chairman of a company that owns a brokerage firm that is a member of the Singapore stock exchange, which was advised of the potential acquisition the day before Lum started buying APL stock. The complaint did not name the brokerage firm.
Charges were first filed by the SEC on April 15 against Ong Congqin Bobby, a Singapore man and, at the time, one other "unknown party."
According to press reports, Ong has said he did not act improperly and expects to be vindicated.

The agency, in its latest complaint filed Friday, also accused a London man, Abdul Ismail, of insider trading. Charges were filed against Ismail in the April 15 complaint, but the agency at that time was not able to identify him because he conducted his trades anonymously through a Swiss account, the SEC alleged.

The SEC alleges Ong and Abdul Ismail bought call options in APL on April 11, prior to the company's public announcement on April 13 that it would be acquired. The agency said both men's options trades represented 74 percent of APL option volume in certain series that day.
-- Singapore newsroom 65-8703080
